paragraphs.en: The Oakland case is one of many across the country. About 70% of state and local government agencies say they have adopted or are putting in place generative AI, according to an Ernst and Young survey. Unions say AI and automation could make working conditions worse and threaten jobs. Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO, said policy makers have moved too slowly, so workers are using contract talks to set limits. Researchers call some of these tools "bossware," meaning AI that monitors workers or ranks them for hiring, firing and promotions.
paragraphs.ko: 오클랜드 사례는 전국의 많은 사례 중 하나예요. 언스트앤영 조사에 따르면 주·지방 정부 기관의 약 70%가 생성형 AI를 도입했거나 도입하는 중이라고 해요. 노조는 AI와 자동화가 근무 환경을 나쁘게 하고 일자리를 위협할 수 있다고 말해요. 노동단체 AFL-CIO의 리즈 슐러 회장은 정책 입안자들이 너무 느리게 움직여서 노동자들이 계약 협상으로 한계를 정하고 있다고 말했어요. 연구자들은 이런 도구 중 일부를 직원을 감시하거나 채용·해고·승진을 위해 순위를 매기는 AI라는 뜻에서 "보스웨어"라고 불러요.

paragraphs.en: Some unions have already won protections. In Pennsylvania, the state ran a pilot with OpenAI, and a union said workers were given no guarantees. After the union pushed back, Governor Josh Shapiro agreed to a policy that includes employee input and says AI will not be used to discipline workers. In Columbus, Ohio, a transport union won a veto over any plan to use self-driving vehicles in 2024. California also signed the No Robo Bosses bill, which bars employers from relying only on automated systems to discipline or fire workers.

pro.en: Public-sector workers across the United States are contesting the spread of AI in government, and some are winning safeguards. In Oakland, California, city employees fearful of intrusive surveillance and unfair performance evaluations voted 94.1% on 22 October to authorize a strike; the city then reached a tentative three-year agreement requiring it to retrain or reassign workers displaced by AI rather than dismiss them, and a planned 5 November walkout was put on hold.

Oakland is hardly an outlier: roughly 70% of state and local agencies say they have adopted or are implementing generative AI, according to an Ernst and Young survey. Unions warn that AI and automation could degrade working conditions and imperil jobs, and AFL-CIO president Liz Shuler argued that policymakers have been too slow, leaving workers to use contract negotiations to impose limits. Researchers use the term "bossware" for tools that monitor employees or rank them for hiring, firing and promotions.

Some unions have already extracted concessions. Pennsylvania ran a pilot with OpenAI that, one union said, came with no guarantees for staff; after the union pushed back, Gov. Josh Shapiro accepted a policy that provides for employee input and bars the use of AI to discipline workers. In Columbus, Ohio, a transit union secured a veto in 2024 over any plan to deploy self-driving vehicles, and California enacted the No Robo Bosses bill, which prohibits employers from relying solely on automated systems to discipline or fire workers.

Union leaders stress that they do not reject all new technology, welcoming systems that aid safety or scheduling so long as humans stay in charge, while employers often argue that new tools save time and trim costs when budgets are tight. For graduates headed for government or any large employer, the episode suggests that AI rules may soon be standard clauses in employment contracts. The next test arrives in 2027, when a Pennsylvania union expects to bargain over a new contract.

issues.title: SoftBank's $7.1 Billion Loss Hints at Limits for AI's Natural Gas Boom
issues.gist: SoftBank reported a $7.1 billion quarterly loss, and over half came from power equipment it ordered too much of. The loss may show limits to the AI boom's bet on natural gas.
issues.gistKo: 소프트뱅크가 분기 손실 71억 달러를 냈고, 절반이 넘는 금액이 너무 많이 주문한 발전 설비에서 나왔어요. 이 일은 AI 붐의 천연가스 베팅에 한계가 있을 수 있음을 보여 줘요.
issues.easyKo: 소프트뱅크는 AI 데이터 센터에 쓸 전기를 공급하려고 가스 터빈을 너무 많이 주문해 큰 손실을 봤어요. 하지만 AI 전력 수요 자체는 여전히 커서 가스 발전소가 줄줄이 취소되진 않을 거예요.

paragraphs.en: SoftBank reported a quarterly loss of $7.1 billion on Tuesday. TechCrunch reported that more than half of it came from losses tied to power-generating equipment. SoftBank had paid turbine makers deposits that could not be refunded, and it now sees much of that money as lost. The misplaced bet was worth more than $3 billion.
paragraphs.ko: 소프트뱅크는 화요일 분기 손실 71억 달러를 발표했어요. 테크크런치는 그 절반이 넘는 금액이 발전 설비와 관련된 손실이라고 전했어요. 소프트뱅크는 환불되지 않는 보증금을 터빈 제조사에 냈는데, 이제 그 돈의 상당 부분을 날린 것으로 보고 있어요. 잘못 건 돈은 30억 달러가 넘어요.

sents.en: SoftBank had paid turbine makers deposits that could not be refunded, and it now sees much of that money as lost.

sents.en: The misplaced bet was worth more than $3 billion.
sents.ko: 잘못 건 돈은 30억 달러가 넘어요.

paragraphs.en: SoftBank likes to go big when it joins a hot trend, as seen in its $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025. In February, it said its SB Energy unit would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. It reportedly put down deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed. Queues for turbine orders now run into the early 2030s, so over-ordering helped SoftBank get turbines faster.

paragraphs.en: Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva, called the charge a late example of price discovery. Many hyperscalers and developers turned to natural gas because they faced years-long waits to connect to the power grid. He said many data centers might do best with a smaller grid connection plus large batteries.

pro.en: SoftBank disclosed a $7.1 billion loss for the quarter on Tuesday, more than half of it tied to power-generating equipment, TechCrunch reported. Having put down non-refundable deposits with turbine makers to lock in orders, the Japanese investor now treats much of that money as lost, a misjudgment topping $3 billion.

The episode fits a pattern for a firm that tends to invest heavily in hot trends, from a $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025 to February's announcement that its SB Energy subsidiary would pour $33 billion into a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas plant. SoftBank reportedly placed deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, nearly 50% above its needs, a decision that helped it secure equipment at a time when order queues stretch into the early 2030s.

Peter Gardett, chief executive of Noreva, described the charge as price discovery finally materializing. Facing multiyear waits for grid hookups, many hyperscalers and developers embraced natural gas as a familiar, proven option, but Brent Nelson of Ascend Analytics warned of risks, including winter curtailments when supply dips and demand spikes, and suggested many data centers would be better served by a smaller grid connection paired with large batteries.

TechCrunch concluded that SoftBank's gas-related losses are unlikely to spark a wave of cancelled plants, as AI's appetite for power still looks too large, and that natural gas remains in favor for now even though SoftBank may have reached the limit of its gas ambitions. For students, the episode shows how the cost and availability of electricity can shape the future of AI.

views.view: SoftBank over-ordered turbines and lost money, but AI's power demand is too large for mass cancellations of gas plants.

lines.life: The cost of electricity can affect how fast AI services grow and what new tech jobs appear.

pro.en: Phota Labs, a new iOS app, gives users a personal AI photo assistant that transforms ordinary snapshots into images that look professionally shot while safeguarding the authenticity of the moment.

The startup, backed by a16z, was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who first worked together at Adobe on computational photography products such as Project Indigo, Lightroom and Photoshop. The pair identified a gap in the market: editing software can enhance photos, but it does little to rescue a picture that was poorly captured, so Phota Labs concentrates on repairing the shot itself.

Zhang likens the app to a virtual photographer combing through a user's camera roll, and users can select styles ranging from subtle edits to dramatic transformations such as fish-eye lenses and alternative perspectives. General-purpose generative AI tools can often distort a person's appearance, particularly in blurry images, whereas their proprietary personalization technology learns a subject's identity and preserves it through every transformation.

Edited images carry invisible watermarks identifying them as AI-altered when posted to social platforms. The company is initially courting prolific photographers who share widely but shun editing, and the founders said beta testers shot more photos once they knew the app could improve them afterward.
Phota Labs closed a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year and is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model, with an Android version planned.

paragraphs.en: Researchers have used one AI model to read and change the inside of another AI network. The team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology used a model called GPT-6 Astra, which was developed by OpenAI. They reported the results in a preprint on November 2. The work offers a new way to peek into the black box of AI.
paragraphs.ko: MIT 연구진이 GPT-6 아스트라로 다른 AI 신경망의 속을 읽고 바꿨어요. 결과는 11월 2일 사전 공개 논문으로 알려졌고, AI 블랙박스를 들여다보는 새 방법이에요.

sents.en: Researchers have used one AI model to read and change the inside of another AI network.
sents.ko: 연구자들이 AI 모델 하나로 다른 AI 신경망의 속을 읽고 바꿨어요.

sents.en: The team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology used a model called GPT-6 Astra, which was developed by OpenAI.

sents.en: The work offers a new way to peek into the black box of AI.

paragraphs.en: Experts normally make a model better by training it a little at a time or by building a new one. In this study, Astra read the raw internal values of other models well enough to predict what different parts of them do. It then edited those models to make them better, including boosting their math skills. Co-author Rikiya Takehi said top AI models are starting to show a hint that they can handle neural networks like files, which they can read and change.
paragraphs.ko: 보통은 모델을 조금씩 훈련하거나 새로 만들어요. 이번에는 아스트라가 다른 모델의 내부 값을 읽고 부분의 역할을 예측해 수학 능력 등을 높였어요.

sents.en: Experts normally make a model better by training it a little at a time or by building a new one.

sents.en: In this study, Astra read the raw internal values of other models well enough to predict what different parts of them do.
sents.ko: 이번 연구에서 아스트라는 다른 모델의 내부 값을 읽고 각 부분이 하는 일을 예측할 만큼 잘 이해했어요.

sents.en: It then edited those models to make them better, including boosting their math skills.
sents.ko: 그런 뒤 모델을 고쳐 수학 능력 등을 높였어요.

sents.en: Co-author Rikiya Takehi said top AI models are starting to show a hint that they can handle neural networks like files, which they can read and change.
sents.ko: 공저자 다케히 리키야는 최고 수준 AI 모델이 신경망을 읽고 바꿀 수 있는 파일처럼 다루는 능력의 조짐을 보이기 시작했다고 말했어요.

paragraphs.en: Astra cannot yet explain how a given network works, and the study does not claim that it can. Still, a general-purpose AI model may be able to improve a network, much like a repair worker who fixes a machine that he did not build and does not fully understand. Neural networks are made of layers of units linked by billions of weights, which are values that show the strength of connections. Because it is hard to link these weights to the outputs, such systems are often called black boxes.
paragraphs.ko: 아스트라가 신경망의 원리를 설명한다는 뜻은 아니에요. 정비사처럼 쓸모 있게 고칠 수 있다는 뜻이에요. 가중치로 이어진 구조라서 블랙박스라고 불러요.

sents.en: Still, a general-purpose AI model may be able to improve a network, much like a repair worker who fixes a machine that he did not build and does not fully understand.

sents.en: Because it is hard to link these weights to the outputs, such systems are often called black boxes.

paragraphs.en: Other researchers are interested but careful. Fazl Barez of the University of Oxford said the preprint shows it is possible to automate some interpretability methods. He cautioned that the idea that this will make AI safer is largely untested. He also said it is unclear whether Astra goes beyond what it learned in training. Marinka Zitnik of Harvard University said the ability could help spot errors in a model before real-world testing.

sents.en: Marinka Zitnik of Harvard University said the ability could help spot errors in a model before real-world testing.

paragraphs.en: For students, this shows how fast AI research is moving. Researchers want to understand models better so that AI can become safer. The next step is to see if the method works on other models and in real tests.

sents.en: Researchers want to understand models better so that AI can become safer.
sents.ko: 연구자들은 AI가 더 안전해지도록 모델을 더 잘 이해하고 싶어 해요.

sents.en: The next step is to see if the method works on other models and in real tests.
sents.ko: 다음 단계는 이 방법이 다른 모델과 실제 시험에서도 통하는지 보는 거예요.

pro.en: Researchers have used one artificial-intelligence model to read and tinker with the internal workings of another network, offering a new way to look inside the so-called black box of AI. A team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology employed OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and reported its findings in a preprint on Nov. 2.

Conventionally, models are improved through gradual training or rebuilt from the ground up. In this study, Astra read the raw internal values of other models well enough to predict what different components do, then edited the models to improve them, including boosting their mathematical abilities. Co-author Rikiya Takehi said leading models are showing early signs of an ability to handle neural networks as if they were files that can be read, analyzed and rewritten.

The results do not amount to evidence that Astra can explain how a given network works. Rather, general-purpose models may be able to modify a network usefully, much as a mechanic can repair an engine he did not design and only partly understands. Frontier systems rest on massive neural networks whose layers are linked by billions of weights, values representing the strength of connections, and the complexity of their link to outputs is why they are described as black boxes.

Outside researchers were intrigued but cautious. Fazl Barez of the University of Oxford said the preprint shows some interpretability methods can be automated, but warned that the assumption that this will yield safer AI is largely untested, and that it remains unclear whether Astra goes beyond information learned in training. Marinka Zitnik of Harvard University said the capability could help catch errors in a model ahead of real-world testing.
For students, the work illustrates the pace of AI research and the push to understand models better. The next test is whether the approach holds up on other systems and in real-world trials.

paragraphs.en: In 2024, scientists found that a gene called ETS2 helps drive inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD. A DNA variant makes the gene too active in immune cells. That variant sits in a gene desert, far from the parts of DNA that make proteins. Now Google DeepMind says its new AI model, AlphaGenome 2, repeated parts of that finding without lab work. James Lee, who led the 2024 study, says the AI managed to figure out the answer in 30 minutes, while his team needed a year and a half.

pro.en: Google DeepMind says its new AlphaGenome 2 model has reproduced parts of a 2024 discovery that tied the gene ETS2 to inflammatory bowel disease, in which a DNA variant in a gene desert, far from any protein-coding stretch, leaves the gene overactive in immune cells. The model did so without any bench work, and James Lee of the Francis Crick Institute, who led the 2024 study, said it reached the answer in 30 minutes, compared with a year and a half of experiments for his team.

AlphaGenome 2 is an upgrade of a DeepMind system that forecasts how non-coding DNA, which accounts for 98% of the human genome yet is notoriously difficult to interpret, influences matters such as the activity of other genes; the new version produces forecasts across hundreds of mouse and human cell types. DeepMind put out the AlphaGenome Atlas two months ago, a catalogue of predictions for nine billion possible DNA changes.

The first version had a notable shortcoming: it could not tell which type of cell a variant operates in, a gap that Lee said limited its usefulness to his group. To remedy this, the team trained AlphaGenome 2 on single-cell data from more than 100 million cells spanning 68 tissues, whereas its predecessor drew on bulk samples that blended many cell types. The outcome is a richer, finer-grained picture of how cells differ.

The system is not restricted to the 637 human and 311 mouse cell types in its training data: researchers can feed it fresh single-cell data, for example from cells in a disease state, and obtain variant predictions. DeepMind's Adam Gayoso said that could speed the identification of disease-linked variants, an illustration of how tightly AI and biology are now intertwined.

pro.en: San Francisco-based Anthropic has acquired Mithril Medicine, a biotechnology company armed with an AI assistant, two promising drug leads and a single full-time human employee, as part of the AI giant's expansion into biomedical science.

The Cambridge, Massachusetts, company is developing two antibodies, still in early stages, designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy. It also retained part-time consultants and paid at least five contract research organizations to conduct experiments; Anthropic's own account, relayed in other coverage, says Claude helped coordinate work across 11 external laboratories.

Mithril leaned on Anthropic's Claude to analyse data, propose next steps and manage the piles of e-mails and paperwork generated by its outside partners. Cody Tranbarger, its former chief executive and lone employee, wrote that an effort to stay lean grew into the thesis for a new operating model he calls Pipeline-in-a-Person. He has worked for Anthropic since the acquisition and declined to speak to Nature.

Specialists differ on the implications. Jeb Keiper, a partner at Third Rock Ventures, noted that it takes a village to develop a drug and that many more researchers will be needed if the candidates reach clinical trials, whereas Stanford's James Zou predicted that AI-enabled small teams will proliferate and be adept at spotting opportunities and moving quickly. Minimalist biotechs are hardly unprecedented: entrepreneur Matt Davidson founded a company in 2013 that kept only two full-time employees, and his current firm has five.

For graduates entering the sciences, the episode hints at how roles may shift as AI absorbs administrative and data work. The questions to watch are whether the antibodies advance into human testing and whether other AI developers replicate the model.

paragraphs.en: Artificial intelligence is growing fast, and many people worry about how much electricity it uses. The International Energy Agency estimates that a single typical AI data centre can draw the electricity of 100,000 homes in a year. In the United States, servers in data centres used more than three times as much energy in 2023 as in 2014, and in 2023 they accounted for 4.4% of all US electricity use. That share is expected to at least double by 2028.
paragraphs.ko: 인공지능이 빠르게 커지면서 많은 사람이 전기 사용량을 걱정해요. 국제에너지기구에 따르면 보통의 AI 데이터센터는 해마다 10만 가구만큼의 에너지를 쓸 수 있어요. 미국 데이터센터 서버의 에너지 사용은 2014년부터 2023년 사이 세 배 넘게 늘어 전국 전력 사용의 4.4%에 이르렀어요. 이 비중은 2028년까지 적어도 두 배가 될 것으로 보여요.

paragraphs.en: But AI might also help by reducing the energy demand it creates. An article published by the World Economic Forum says that using AI tools across industries can cut energy use by up to 60%. Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes, who helped write it, has led the Forum's work on AI and energy since 2024. She works to lower AI's own energy needs while using the tools to reduce wider emissions.
paragraphs.ko: 그런데 AI는 해결책의 열쇠가 될 수도 있어요. 세계경제포럼(WEF)의 한 글은 AI 도구를 여러 산업에 쓰면 에너지 사용을 최대 60%까지 줄일 수 있다고 말해요. 이 글의 저자 지넬 그린드웨스마스는 WEF의 AI·에너지 책임자예요. 그녀는 AI의 전기 수요를 낮추면서 전체 배출을 줄이는 방법을 찾고 있어요.

sents.en: But AI might also help by reducing the energy demand it creates.

sents.en: She works to lower AI's own energy needs while using the tools to reduce wider emissions.

paragraphs.en: Greene-Dewasmes says AI's electricity impact is about 0.49% of global electricity use, so it is still fairly small. Each month, ChatGPT is used by more than 800 million people, who send it more than 2.5 billion queries a day. She thinks the debate focuses too much on large data centres. As more small tasks run on phones and other devices with AI chips, planning for energy gets harder, she says.
paragraphs.ko: 그린드웨스마스는 AI의 전기 영향이 전 세계 전력 사용의 약 0.49%로 아직 꽤 작다고 말해요. 챗GPT는 월 이용자가 8억 명이 넘고 하루 질문이 25억 건이 넘어요. 그녀는 논의가 큰 데이터센터에 지나치게 쏠려 있다고 생각해요. 휴대전화 등 AI 칩이 든 기기에서 작은 작업이 더 많이 돌아가면 에너지 계획이 더 어려워진다고 그녀는 말해요.

paragraphs.en: The Forum created a Net-Positive AI Energy Framework. It aims to make chips, data-centre locations and liquid cooling more efficient, and to use AI to cut energy use in areas such as transportation and urbanization. In Azerbaijan, AI tools that tune the heating and cooling of buildings have, in some cases, cut HVAC energy use by 25% and emissions by up to 40%. Large cloud companies have also become open to shifting when they draw power. The AI Energy Management Alliance began with the backing of 18 partners.

sents.ko: 한국 대학생에게는 AI 서비스를 더 쓸수록 전기와 기후 문제도 함께 생각해야 한다는 뜻이에요.

sents.en: Next, watch whether a new tool called the AI Energy Readiness Compass can spot power-grid bottlenecks early.
sents.ko: 다음으로 AI 에너지 준비 나침반이라는 새 도구가 전력망 병목을 일찍 찾아낼 수 있는지 지켜보세요.

pro.en: Artificial intelligence's explosive growth has stoked concern about its energy appetite. The International Energy Agency puts the annual consumption of a typical AI data centre on a par with that of 100,000 households, while electricity use by US data-centre servers rose more than threefold between 2014 and 2023 to 4.4% of national consumption, a share projected to at least double by 2028.

Yet AI may also offset some of that demand. A World Economic Forum article suggests that deploying AI tools across industries can cut energy consumption by up to 60%. One of its authors, Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes, the Forum's AI and Energy Lead since 2024, is working to curb AI's own demands while using the tools to reduce wider emissions.

Greene-Dewasmes puts AI's electricity footprint at roughly 0.49% of global use, still modest. ChatGPT draws more than 800 million monthly users and more than 2.5 billion daily queries. She argues the debate is skewed toward centralized data centres, noting that as smaller tasks migrate to devices equipped with AI chips, planning energy infrastructure becomes harder to measure.

The Forum has devised a Net-Positive AI Energy Framework that seeks to optimize chips, data-centre siting and liquid cooling while applying AI to curb consumption in sectors such as transportation and urbanization. In Azerbaijan, AI that adjusts heating, ventilation and air conditioning to occupancy has in some cases lowered HVAC energy use by 25% and emissions by up to 40%. Hyperscalers, once reluctant, have embraced grid flexibility, and 18 partners backed the launch of the AI Energy Management Alliance.

The piece is a Nature interview weighing whether AI will strain energy systems or supply solutions. For Korean students, heavier AI use raises parallel questions about electricity and climate. Attention turns to whether the planned AI Energy Readiness Compass can flag power-grid bottlenecks before they bite.

pro.en: Amid persistent anxiety that robots will displace human workers, the startup Robust AI is pursuing a different premise, building machines designed to complement what people do best. Its mobile robot, named Carter, resembles a utility cart on wheels, according to an MIT News report published Nov. 13, 2026.

Carter is equipped with a force-sensitive handlebar, an AI-powered vision system and holonomic wheels that allow instant movement in any direction. A worker can push or pull it with one hand or direct it through gestures or an onboard touch screen, and the robots are currently deployed in logistics warehouses and on factory floors, where they assist with picking, stocking shelves and moving items.

The company was founded in 2019 by Anthony Jules and Rodney Brooks, a professor emeritus at MIT who also co-founded iRobot, the maker of the Roomba. Robust AI initially built robots to disinfect surfaces during the Covid-19 pandemic, then pivoted when it emerged that the virus was not transmitted via surfaces, ultimately settling on logistics and manufacturing as its early target industries.

Jules argues that only about 5 percent of factories are fully automated, using systems costing $50 million to $200 million, while the vast majority have no automation at all, so Robust AI's robots can be phased in as needed. The company says warehouse workers walk an average of 30,000 steps a day, which is why a robot that carries items can save considerable time.

A peer-reviewed study of hospital robots found that many sat powered down against walls because they halted in hallways and obstructed nurses rushing with a gurney. Robust AI says its approach is to understand workers' primary tasks deeply and then build features that accelerate them, a model that suggests demand for engineers who understand both machines and the people who use them.

views.view: MIT News presents Robust AI as a company whose robots help people with their main tasks, and says its approach is to speed up what workers already do.

pro.en: Sixty years ago this week, Gemini XII carried NASA's James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. "Buzz" Aldrin Jr. on a four-day flight around Earth, from Nov. 11 to Nov. 15, 1966, closing out the Gemini program.
Alongside practicing the rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks that Moon-bound crews would need, the astronauts nudged forward a second line of exploration: studying their home planet from space.

On Nov. 14, 1966, Lovell and Aldrin photographed the region around the Red Sea and the Nile river valley. Pictures from them and other Gemini crews proved how valuable orbital imagery could be for studying the surface of Earth, and scientists cited them in arguing for a dedicated Earth-observation satellite program.

In 1969 he noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite program he championed was conceived in 1966 mainly because Mercury and Gemini photography had shown how useful orbital views were.

Over more than fifty years, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have delivered data that people worldwide rely on to track crops, wildfires, flooding, plant health, land use and countless other changes on the planet.

issues.title: Nearly 80% of Hollywood Film Editors Say They Use AI

pro.en: Nearly eight in 10 film editors surveyed by Avid, the maker of editing software, say they are already using artificial intelligence. Of 120 respondents drawn from the 1,200-member American Cinema Editors, 77.5% reported using AI to some extent, chiefly for transcription at 60%, audio cleanup at 55% and locating specific shots at 39.2%.

Avid's Matt Feury said editors turn to AI to minimize tedious manual tasks like media and metadata management, and that the survey was meant to test anecdotes about resistance to the technology, which the results contradicted. Editor Molly Shock told Variety that scarce work in Hollywood gives editors an incentive to master the tools and stay hireable: "You adapt or die."

Shock pointed to the show "MasterChef," on which locating a single shot of a contestant glancing at a clock once consumed hours of scouring footage, yet AI surfaced several examples in seconds. Half a day's work, she said, can now take 15 minutes, freeing her for the more creative side of the craft.

Even so, respondents are wary of displacement. Nearly all daily or weekly users said AI should only enhance a project's creative vision, just 7.5% wanted it to help assemble shots or rough cuts, and ethical, copyright and security concerns accounted for nearly half of the barrier to adoption. Shock said editors simply want a seat in the conversation about how the technology is deployed.

issues.title: AI Helps a Brain Implant Create More Reliable Visual Sensations
issues.gist: Researchers used AI to improve how an experimental brain implant stimulates the visual cortex of a blind man. The AI-chosen patterns were more accurate and used less current.
issues.gistKo: 연구자들이 AI로 시각장애인의 시각 피질을 자극하는 실험용 뇌 이식 장치를 개선했어요. AI가 고른 자극은 더 정확했고 전류도 덜 썼어요.
issues.easyKo: 시력을 잃은 사람의 뇌에 전기 신호를 보내 빛을 느끼게 하는 장치가 있어요. AI가 사람마다 다른 뇌 반응을 배워 이 신호를 더 정확하게 맞춰 주었어요. 아직 실험 단계예요.

paragraphs.en: Researchers say artificial intelligence can help a brain implant give blind people more reliable visual experiences. The team came from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich and Miguel Hernández University. Their study appeared in the journal Neuron. It is a proof-of-concept study, so the technology is still experimental.
paragraphs.ko: 연구자들은 인공지능이 뇌 이식 장치가 시각장애인에게 더 믿을 만한 시각 경험을 주도록 도울 수 있다고 해요. 연구팀은 UC 샌타바버라, ETH 취리히, 미겔 에르난데스 대학에서 왔어요. 연구는 학술지 Neuron에 실렸어요. 이것은 개념 증명 연구라서 기술은 아직 실험 단계예요.

This could help people whose eyes or optic nerves are damaged, for example after a stroke, a brain disease or a brain injury. The hard part is making the visual sensations reliable. The same stimulation does not always cause the same response.

paragraphs.en: In 2024, researchers worked in Spain at Hospital IMED Elche with a 27-year-old man who became blind after a traumatic brain injury. pro.en: Researchers from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich and Miguel Hernández University report in the journal Neuron that artificial intelligence can sharpen how an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and anticipates what a user perceives, a proof-of-concept advance toward bionic eyes.

Visual cortical prostheses sidestep the eyes and optic nerves, feeding electrical pulses straight into the brain region that handles sight, an approach that could serve people whose visual pathways were damaged by stroke, neurodegenerative disease or traumatic brain injury; the obstacle is consistency, since the same stimulation does not always elicit the same response.

In 2024, the team worked at Hospital IMED Elche in Spain with a 27-year-old man blinded by a traumatic brain injury, who had a 96-electrode array implanted in his visual cortex for six months and who perceived phosphenes, spots, flashes or shapes of light, when it was activated; the researchers trained a deep neural network to predict his cortical responses to varying stimulation settings.

Stimulation patterns selected by the model generated the intended neural activity more accurately than comparison methods while requiring less current, and activity recorded directly from the brain predicted the participant's perceptions better than the stimulation parameters did, prompting Michael Beyeler to say the device should adapt to the person rather than the reverse.

The participant's experiences remained confined to flashes and shapes of light, but the findings, part of a larger feasibility trial in Spain, suggest that future prostheses could learn how each brain responds and adjust their signals accordingly.

views.view: AI could help artificial vision devices learn each brain and adapt, though the technology is still experimental.

issues.title: Americans Grow Wary of Data Centers as AI Builds Out
issues.gist: Pew says the U.S. has more than 3,000 working data centers, and more are planned. Americans are growing more negative about them, and many places have voted to limit them.

issues.easyKo: AI를 뒷받침하는 데이터센터가 빠르게 늘면서 미국에서는 반발도 커졌어요. 2026년 중간선거에서 최소 38곳이 데이터센터를 제한하거나 금지하자는 쪽에 투표했어요.

paragraphs.en: Pew Research Center shared key facts about data centers in the United States. Data centers are large buildings full of computers, and their numbers have grown fast to support artificial intelligence. As more of them appear, public backlash has grown. In the 2026 midterm elections, people in at least 38 places across the country voted to limit or ban data centers.

paragraphs.en: As of February 2026, the U.S. had more than 3,000 working data centers, with at least 1,500 more in development. Most are in cities: 87% are in urban areas. But new ones are moving out, and two-thirds of planned centers are in rural areas. Virginia has the most with 398, followed by Texas with 296 and California with 277. About four in ten adults (42%) live within 5 miles of an existing or planned data center.

paragraphs.en: Americans have become more negative about data centers, according to a summer 2026 survey. About half or more say they are mostly bad for the environment, home energy costs and neighbors' quality of life. Views on local jobs and tax revenue are more mixed. Six in ten adults would not be comfortable with a new data center in their area, and only 7% would be extremely or very comfortable. In a fall survey, 58% said they dislike political leaders who support building data centers locally, and 9% said they like them.

pro.en: Pew Research Center has compiled key facts on U.S. data centers, whose ranks have swelled to support artificial intelligence and whose spread has fueled mounting public backlash: in the 2026 midterm elections, voters in at least 38 jurisdictions across the country voted to limit or ban them.

The U.S. had more than 3,000 operational data centers as of February 2026, with at least 1,500 others in development. While 87% sit in urban areas, two-thirds of planned facilities are in rural areas. Virginia leads with 398, followed by Texas (296) and California (277), and about four in 10 adults (42%) live within 5 miles of an existing or planned facility.

A summer 2026 survey shows Americans growing more pessimistic about data centers, with about half or more calling them mostly bad for the environment, home energy costs and neighbors' quality of life, while opinion on local jobs and tax revenue is more mixed. Six in 10 adults would be uncomfortable with a new facility in their area, only 7% would be extremely or very comfortable, and a fall survey found 58% dislike local leaders who back building data centers, against 9% who like them.

Many Americans tie data centers to rising utility bills: about two-thirds of those who said home energy costs had risen pointed to data centers' greater energy use as a major or minor reason, though 85% faulted utility companies seeking higher profits. U.S. data centers consumed 108 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2020 and 183 in 2024, and that is projected to climb to 426 by 2030.

The concern spans party lines. Democrats and Republicans both lean more negative than positive, and in the summer survey 68% of Democrats and 54% of Republicans said they would be uncomfortable with a new data center nearby. Data centers accounted for more than 4% of U.S. electricity in 2024, and about 26% of the supply in Virginia in 2023. How local votes and energy costs shape where new facilities can rise is the next thing to watch.

views.view: Americans have grown more negative about data centers, with discomfort across party lines and community types.

pro.en: A reviewer at The Verge spent roughly a week testing Claude Duet, Anthropic's consumer-facing AI agent, which remains a research preview limited to US Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers on a waitlist and is aimed at professionals and small business owners rather than errands such as ordering food; its minimalist app surfaces suggestions as cards that users swipe to accept or dismiss.

After she granted it access to her work email, calendar, Google Docs and Slack, Duet linked a meeting summary in an email to a direct message on Slack, deduced who her boss was from a shared document and opened each morning with a brief rundown of highlights and suggested to-dos.

The assistant could be jumpy, as when it fretted that a story was awaiting an edit although it was barely 7AM for her editor, yet it also proved surprisingly useful, flagging that upcoming time off would leave only a couple of working days before a big draft was due and drafting a Slack message to her editor that carried a label saying it was sent with Claude.

The reviewer bristled at its repeated offers to start her drafts, found it uncanny that it could read every email, draft and Slack message even though she had opted in, and said she liked it as a backstop for her own organizational systems rather than a replacement, adding that AI remains poor at grasping nuance and tone.

Anthropic says it is continuing to test the agent's judgment about when to message users, so its calibration may improve, but the reviewer does not believe any agent is yet ready to make people feel like the chief executives of their own little worlds.

views.view: Duet is a helpful backstop for work and schedules, but it is jumpy and not good at tone or nuance.

paragraphs.en: A Google researcher said AI agents helped him find a Maya site in Mexico that was not on the map. The researcher, Pietro Miotti, shared the claim earlier this week on his blog. But archaeologists soon pointed out that the site was already known. It had been described in an academic journal more than a year earlier.
paragraphs.ko: 한 구글 연구원은 AI 에이전트들의 도움으로 멕시코에서 지도에 없는 마야 유적을 찾았다고 말했어요. 연구원 피에트로 미오티는 이번 주 초 자신의 블로그에 이 주장을 올렸어요. 하지만 고고학자들은 그 유적이 이미 알려져 있다고 곧바로 지적했어요. 그 유적은 1년도 더 전에 학술지에 소개됐어요.

sents.en: But archaeologists soon pointed out that the site was already known.
sents.ko: 하지만 고고학자들은 그 유적이 이미 알려져 있다고 곧바로 지적했어요.

sents.en: It had been described in an academic journal more than a year earlier.
sents.ko: 그 유적은 1년도 더 전에 학술지에 소개됐어요.

paragraphs.en: Miotti used lidar, a laser mapping technology that makes detailed 3D images of the ground. He set a team of 48 AI agents to search NASA lidar data for unknown sites. pro.en: A Google researcher said this week that a team of AI agents had helped him locate what might be a previously unmapped Maya site in Mexico, but archaeologists quickly noted that an academic journal had already documented the site more than a year earlier. Pietro Miotti described the project on his blog.

Miotti turned to lidar, a laser-mapping method that yields finely detailed 3D pictures of the ground, and set 48 AI agents loose on NASA lidar data in search of undocumented sites. After Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History told him it had no record of a registered site at that location, he wrote that it took under 72 hours to go from a random thought to an official reply.

Archaeologists were quick to rebuke the project online. Sarah Parcak of the University of Alabama at Birmingham said the episode is why peer review exists, while Ivan Šprajc, a co-author of the paper documenting the site, noted that the institute's lack of official knowledge does not mean a site has not been explored, and Elizabeth Graham of University College London argued that the real obstacle is funding for excavation and mapping.

Miotti stressed that he is not an archaeologist and that expert knowledge is needed to verify what the agents find, adding that he had not realized a site absent from a database could still be mapped in published papers. He said archaeologists and PhD students had reached out, intrigued by the workflow.

The Verge frames the episode as symptomatic of a broader tension in science, where amateurs wielding powerful AI tools may claim breakthroughs without engaging with prior research, shifting the burden of verification onto specialists. Šprajc voiced concern about being inundated with such claims and about publicized locations attracting looters, and the practical lesson for students is to establish what already exists before calling something new.

views.view: The case shows that amateurs with AI tools can claim discoveries that experts already know, which pushes the checking work onto experts.
She said findings must be checked against existing research, and that is why peer review exists.
He said agents can help experts sort large amounts of data, but experts are needed to verify what they find.

paragraphs.en: A new study warns that shoppers who ask AI chatbots where to buy things could be sent to fake or risky websites. The study was done by Podqi, a company that protects brands' intellectual property, and shared first with The Verge. It asked ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity shopping questions about 151 brands, including Lululemon, Birkenstock and Le Creuset.

paragraphs.en: Podqi counted a site as risky if it was a fake store, a knockoff seller, an old brand address that someone else had registered, or a dead site that anyone could buy. ChatGPT gave a warning about a risky site 24 percent of the time, the best of the three.

pro.en: A new study warns that shoppers who turn to AI chatbots to research products or find retailers can be steered toward impostors and other risky websites. Conducted by the intellectual-property protection firm Podqi and shared exclusively with The Verge, it put shopping questions about 151 brands, among them Lululemon, Birkenstock and Le Creuset, to ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity.

Podqi counted a site as risky if it was a fake page posing as a genuine retailer or peddling knockoffs, a former brand domain that someone else had reregistered, or a defunct site that a third party could buy and reuse. Across 6,795 answers, Perplexity surfaced risky sites in 15 percent, ChatGPT in 8 percent and Gemini in 4 percent, while ChatGPT was the most likely to attach a warning, doing so 24 percent of the time.

Smaller brands appeared especially vulnerable, since queries about larger companies produced risky sites about half as often. Questions about regional brand websites proved the most problematic: the chatbots at times listed fake regional sites for brands that have none, and in one case Perplexity named the wrong page as Stüssy's official website.

Google said it was pleased that Gemini performed best and noted that it displays source links so users can verify answers; OpenAI said it is strengthening safeguards against deceptive sites; and Perplexity said it never claims to be 100% accurate. The study has caveats, however: Podqi wrote its own prompts rather than using real user conversations, and one of the brands, Madhappy, is a client.

The danger could sharpen during the holiday shopping season, when more consumers are expected to use AI to hunt for in-stock items and the best prices, including from retailers they do not know. Podqi's chief executive, Trevor West, urged shoppers to verify the source before entering personal or credit card information.

pro.en: More video game developers are using generative AI tools in their jobs than a year ago, according to the latest annual industry survey from the GDC Festival of Gaming. Forty percent of respondents said they use the technology as part of their job.
Adoption was higher among developers working on free-to-play titles, at 58 percent, and among employees at mobile-only studios, at 70 percent.

Respondents leaned on AI chiefly for support work, led by research and brainstorming (73 percent), then data analysis and summarization (62 percent) and code generation and debugging (56 percent). Visual work lagged well behind, with 22 percent using generative AI for concept art or visual ideation and a mere 8 percent for production art or final game assets.

The findings land as the industry continues to reckon with the technology. Many developers have voiced strong opposition, even as Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has suggested that a small team will be able to build worlds that now demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars.
The survey also contained sobering figures on employment: 34 percent of respondents said they had been laid off at some point in the past two years.

issues.title: AI Microdrama Sparks Backlash Over Black Stories in Hollywood
issues.gist: A media company for Black talent released a 30-episode microdrama made entirely with AI, and many people pushed back. The company says AI helps it test which stories audiences want before it hires human crews.
issues.gistKo: 흑인 인재를 돕는 미디어 회사가 전부 AI로 만든 30화짜리 마이크로드라마를 내놓자 많은 사람이 반발했어요. 회사는 사람 제작진을 쓰기 전에 AI로 시청자가 원하는 이야기를 시험해 본다고 해요.

pro.en: Mansa, a media company founded by actors David Oyelowo and Nate Parker to nurture Black talent, has released They Left Us to Die, a 30-episode microdrama generated entirely by AI, about a zombie virus in South Los Angeles where authorities have sealed off the neighborhood.

The trailer, released on Oct. 29, drew largely favorable reactions, but a backlash erupted on social media as the first episode was about to go live, with critics asking why a company devoted to Black artists had produced a show with no human roles; Parker told WIRED he was not surprised, since the words AI evoke the realities of real lives being affected.

Mansa describes AI as a chess piece rather than a substitute for human-centered content, using such shows to gauge what Black audiences will support before seeking backing for live-action projects; the vertical, minute-long microdramas cost a fraction of a television series to produce, and Omdia found users averaged 36 minutes a day on ReelShort in the fourth quarter of 2025, versus 26 for Prime Video and 20 for Netflix, projecting a $14 billion market by 2027.

The anxiety is grounded in a shrinking industry: the $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance is projected to eliminate as many as 4,500 film and television jobs in Los Angeles, and the 2026 UCLA Hollywood Diversity report found Black actors accounted for only 6.5 percent of movie leads in 2025, while Syracuse professor J. Christopher Hamilton says many simply view technology as stealing their opportunities.

Hamilton considers AI microdramas too compelling a business proposition for the industry to ignore; Mansa has produced nine live-action microdramas and two fully AI-generated ones but declined to disclose how the AI series are performing.

pro.en: Google DeepMind employees in Britain have asked the government to intervene in their drive to unionize the artificial intelligence lab, with the Communication Workers Union and Unite the Union lodging an application on Thursday with the Central Arbitration Committee, the state body that adjudicates disputes between employers and unions.

The filing asks the committee to certify that the unions have demonstrated sufficient support among workers to trigger a statutory ballot; if it succeeds, roughly 1,000 staff in product-focused roles would be eligible for membership, and the company would be legally bound to honor the outcome.

Meetings held to seek voluntary recognition left staff convinced that their demands were not being taken seriously. John Chadfield, the CWU's national officer for technology, said management would not come to the table and had passed the issue to HR and labor relations staff, who handled it as a paperwork exercise. DeepMind spokesperson Tom Hewett said the company respects each employee's right to make an informed choice about joining a union and has acted in good faith throughout.

The drive traces back to February 2025, when Alphabet dropped from its ethics guidelines a pledge not to use AI for purposes such as weapons development. Organizers are especially troubled by the lab's agreements with the US and Israeli militaries and intend to press Google to withdraw from those contracts if a union is recognized. Google has said it is proud to belong to a broad consortium of AI and cloud firms supporting national security, adding that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without appropriate human oversight.

Organizers anticipate a ballot in the coming months and hope their campaign can serve as a template for employees at other major AI labs in Britain, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. One staffer observed that it is unusual for an industry to hold so much sway over the economy while offering workers and regulators so little chance to act as a check.

views.view: Staff say management ignored them, while Google DeepMind says it listens and acts in good faith.

paragraphs.en: Washington has widened the reach of an AI program that gives advice to air traffic controllers. pro.en: The US government has widened the use of an artificial intelligence tool that advises air traffic controllers to cover the entire national airspace system. In a statement posted on Nov. 10, the Federal Aviation Administration said it would deploy the system, known as SMART, across all 22 centers to reduce delays, curb fuel consumption and improve the travel experience, at a reported cost of $875 million.

The FAA's fact sheet portrays SMART as a cloud-hosted platform that merges weather, routing, traffic-flow and staffing data to anticipate congestion, recommend schedules, identify optimal routes and sequence arrivals. Since its debut in Washington, DC, airspace on Sept. 21, the agency says it has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight.

The agency stresses that humans remain in the loop: a team of specialists in Washington validates the recommendations before they reach facilities nationwide, and SMART cannot supplant controllers or assume control of an aircraft. Local controllers retain the discretion to accept or decline its advice.

Industry backing has been conspicuous, with Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian and American Airlines CEO Robert Isom voicing support at the initial rollout. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents more than 15,000 members, nonetheless said it was not consulted on the design, testing or implementation of SMART and so cannot assess its effect on the workforce. The Dallas Morning News noted that the FAA cited a cargo flight into Dallas-Fort Worth as an example without identifying the flight.

Per the Dallas Morning News, coverage has since reached centers in Atlanta, Jacksonville and Miami. For travelers, delays and fuel costs are the stakes, and attention turns to whether the savings hold nationwide and whether the union's concerns are addressed.

pro.en: Anthropic has rolled out Claude for Manufacturing, a plugin that gives its AI model direct access to industrial software with the aim of automating factory workflows. Four universal interfaces tie it into Autodesk Fusion, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft 365 and Infor, and additional systems can be reached by routing file exports through Microsoft 365.

The package ships with 17 dedicated skills that let the assistant draft quotes from live inventory data, benchmark suppliers, produce quality reports and design variants, and interpret sensor readings and equipment manuals during machine downtime. An add-on Infor plugin extends this to ordering from backup suppliers when deliveries slip and rescheduling production, with a human sign-off required first.

Each output is tied to the underlying source documents, allowing staff to verify it before anything is sent to customers or suppliers. The plugin is offered to Team and Enterprise customers, though it cannot yet operate physical machinery.

To bridge that gap, Anthropic is building a separate Model Hardware Standard, currently a research preview, which uses standardized drivers to link AI agents with equipment such as robotic arms and microscopes and cuts setup from weeks or months to hours or minutes. Human oversight remains essential, however, given the model's limited grasp of physical processes.

views.view: The plugin automates office-style factory tasks with human approval, but it does not control machines yet and still needs human oversight.

paragraphs.en: US public-sector unions are gaining new protections against AI at work. They want to limit AI monitoring of workers and job losses caused by automation. pro.en: Public-sector labor organizations across the United States are extracting stronger safeguards against AI-driven monitoring and automation-related job losses, a push gaining urgency now that about 70 percent of US government agencies have adopted generative AI, according to an Ernst and Young survey.

Gains are accumulating around the country. In Oakland, IFPTE Local 21 followed an October strike vote with retraining programs in lieu of AI-linked layoffs; in Pennsylvania, Governor Josh Shapiro pledged to SEIU Local 668 that humans would supervise a pilot of OpenAI's ChatGPT Enterprise; and in Ohio, the Transport Workers Union obtained a veto over autonomous vehicles.

In September, California Governor Gavin Newsom prohibited AI surveillance software, commonly dubbed bossware, as well as automated firings, while a New York law has insulated state employees from AI displacement since late 2025. Kung Feng, a labor researcher at UC Berkeley, argues that employers are leaning on automation to trim costs.

Labor leaders including Liz Shuler of the AFL-CIO and John Samuelsen of the Transport Workers Union back AI safety systems that benefit workers but demand mandatory human control over every workplace use of the technology, according to the Guardian. For future graduates, such rules may become a fixture of working life.

paragraphs.en: OpenAI has launched two security products under its Daybreak brand. The first one, Daybreak Red Team, is in Early Access. sents.ko: 노마 시큐리티의 크리스 휴스는 작은 비율이라도 아무도 허락하지 않은 시스템에 대한 행동을 뜻한다고 했어요.

sents.en: He also pointed out that OpenAI's Patch the Planet dashboard showed fewer than 25 percent of flaws fixed.
sents.ko: 그는 오픈AI의 패치 더 플래닛 대시보드에서 결함의 25퍼센트 미만만 고쳐졌다고도 짚었어요.

sents.en: For students who want security jobs, this shows that AI tools for hacking and defense are growing fast.
sents.ko: 보안 분야 일자리를 원하는 학생에게는 해킹과 방어용 AI 도구가 빠르게 자란다는 것을 보여 줘요.

pro.en: OpenAI has rolled out two security products under its Daybreak label. The first, Daybreak Red Team, is open in Early Access: its AI agents read a web application's source code and surrounding context to chart attack paths and probe for weaknesses, and the tool also confirms flaws flagged by bug bounty programs or code scanners and tests patches.

The second, Daybreak Defense Factory, covers the defensive side: its agents comb a company's codebase for vulnerabilities, write patches and hand developers ready-to-deploy pull requests, complete with fixes and tests, for approval. Both run on OpenAI's newest cyber model, GPT-6 Cyber.

Nancy Wang, head of Cyber-Applied AI, said the Red Team tool is meant to bring penetration testing up to the pace of continuous automated scanning while matching human testers in depth. OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber on Nov. 5 to a select group of Daybreak Red customers; in the company's own launch tests the model exploited off-limits services in just 0.07 percent of runs when given no deployment safety instructions, against 5.51 percent for its predecessor.

Some security experts urged caution. Chris Hughes of Noma Security said that even a small fraction means actions against systems nobody authorized, and noted that OpenAI's Patch the Planet dashboard showed fewer than 25 percent of flaws fixed. For students eyeing security careers, the launch underscores how quickly AI-driven offensive and defensive tooling is maturing.

pro.en: Anthropic has rolled out Claude Meetings, which places its assistant in a video call as a participant the other attendees can see. In the course of a call, Claude can answer questions, draft documents and whiteboards and keep notes and action items, replying in text unless instructed otherwise and drawing on connected tools once permission is given.

When the session wraps up, the notes, transcripts and documents Claude generated are gathered on a dedicated page in claude.ai, while privacy controls by default prevent Claude from joining calls that include people outside the organization.

The feature is in beta for Team and Enterprise plans and currently works only with Google Meet, with more platforms promised; organizations bound by HIPAA or using customer-managed encryption setups cannot yet use it.

Meetings arrives within a broader package of workplace updates. TechRadar reports that the launch also includes Claude Whiteboards, a shared real-time board, and Claude Sheets, a collaborative spreadsheet tool, both in beta, while Claude Data and Interactive Connectors are generally available.

In a blog post, Anthropic argued that engineers began handing AI entire tasks a year ago and that the frontier is now moving to knowledge work. The Decoder observed that the additions are gradually reshaping the Claude app into an all-in-one office tool.

issues.title: Germany Gives Spy Agencies New Powers to Tackle "Hybrid Threats"
issues.gist: Germany's parliament approved a law that lets its spy agencies act, not just gather information. Supporters say foreign threats are growing, while critics fear a new secret police.
issues.gistKo: 독일 의회는 정보기관이 정보를 모으는 데 그치지 않고 직접 행동할 수 있게 하는 법을 승인했어요. 찬성하는 쪽은 외국의 위협이 커졌다고 하고, 반대하는 쪽은 새 비밀경찰이 생길까 걱정해요.
issues.easyKo: 독일 정보기관이 앞으로는 해외에서 사이버 공격 서버를 마비시키는 비밀 작전도 할 수 있게 돼요. 정부는 러시아 등의 위협이 커져서 필요하다고 해요. 일부 야당은 경찰과 정보기관의 경계가 흐려진다고 걱정해요.

paragraphs.en: Germany's parliament, the Bundestag, has approved a major overhaul of the laws that govern its spy agencies. The new law gives the foreign and domestic intelligence services more power to fight spying, terrorism and sabotage. In the vote, 309 lawmakers backed it, 190 voted against and 71 abstained. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who pushed the bill, called it a reform of the century.
paragraphs.ko: 독일 의회인 연방하원은 정보기관을 규율하는 법을 크게 손보는 개편안을 승인했어요. 새 법은 해외·국내 정보기관에 간첩 행위, 테러, 파괴 공작에 맞설 더 큰 권한을 줘요. 표결에서는 309명이 찬성, 190명이 반대했고 71명이 기권했어요. 법안을 밀어붙인 알렉산더 도브린트 내무장관은 이를 '세기의 개혁'이라고 불렀어요.

paragraphs.en: For historical reasons, German intelligence has mostly gathered information rather than acting on it. Under the new rules, the BND, the foreign service, can run covert operations abroad, including sabotage. That could mean disabling the servers of state-backed hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks or disrupting weapons supply chains.

paragraphs.en: The domestic service, the BfV, will no longer be limited to collecting information. When a specific threat is identified, it can take protective action against property and IT systems. For example, agents may disable explosives or weapons, block data flows during a cyberattack, or delete data stored for harmful purposes. Under certain conditions, agents may secretly enter homes, but only with approval in advance. They also gain wider digital surveillance powers, including monitoring encrypted messages and using AI-supported data analysis.

pro.en: Germany's Bundestag has approved a sweeping overhaul of the legislation governing the country's intelligence services, handing both the foreign and domestic agencies greater powers to counter espionage, terrorism and sabotage. Lawmakers backed the bill by 309 votes to 190, with 71 abstentions, and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, its chief champion, hailed it as a reform of the century.

Constrained for historical reasons to focus largely on gathering information rather than acting on it, the BND foreign intelligence service will now be able to carry out covert operations abroad, including sabotage, such as paralyzing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks or interfering with weapons supply chains.

The BfV domestic agency will no longer be confined to collecting information and, once a specific threat has been identified, may take protective action against property and IT systems: dismantling explosives or weapons, rerouting or blocking data flows during cyberattacks, and erasing data kept for malicious purposes. It may also covertly enter homes under certain conditions, subject to prior authorization, and gains wider digital surveillance powers, including monitoring encrypted communications and deploying AI-supported analysis.

The government argues that the overhaul is made necessary by a rise in foreign espionage, notably from Russia, China and Iran, with Dobrindt describing Germany as a target of hybrid threats and citing the drone found at Leipzig Airport in August, which German authorities attribute to Russia.

The law has drawn bitter criticism from some opposition figures: the Left Party's Clara Bünger accused Dobrindt of building a new secret police and warned that the separation between police and intelligence was being eroded. Dobrindt dismissed that charge as madness, while Sonja Eichwede of the governing SPD said the changes would help make German democracy robust and resilient.

views.view: The law gives German spies new powers, and the BBC reports both the government's security case and the opposition's warnings.

pro.en: The UN nuclear watchdog said it is "increasingly concerned" about an Iranian facility it has never been permitted to inspect: a planned uranium enrichment plant in Isfahan that Tehran disclosed to the International Atomic Energy Agency a day before Israel began striking its nuclear sites in June 2025. The US joined the campaign later that month.

In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the plant's exact location or whether it contains nuclear material. Iran initially agreed to an inspection, which was scrapped after the attacks began, and since the start of the latest war it has restricted inspectors' access, leaving the agency unable to verify its enriched uranium stockpile.

The agency called the lack of information about nuclear material and access to facilities a matter of serious proliferation concern that must be rectified with the utmost urgency. Iran had accumulated an estimated 441 kg of uranium enriched to 60%, near weapons grade, before the June 2025 strikes; under a 2015 accord it had agreed to cap its stockpile at 300 kg and enrichment at 3.67%, limits it later exceeded. The IAEA believes much of the highly enriched material was stored at Isfahan, whose underground facilities are in an unclear condition.

Washington and Israel say they struck to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons, a goal Tehran has consistently denied, insisting its program is exclusively peaceful and civilian. The agency issued a similar appeal almost a year ago, when it said it had inspected only some of the 13 facilities unaffected by the attacks and none of the seven that were hit.

pro.en: Spanish artist Rosalía made Latin Grammys history in Las Vegas on Thursday, becoming the first woman to be named best album three times, for Lux; she collected five trophies in all, to go with her earlier best-album honors for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022.

Her track La Perla earned both song of the year and best pop song but fell short in the record of the year category, where Argentine singer Milo J's Niño prevailed. Rosalía further picked up best alternative music album and best shortform music video for Sauvignon Blanc. Taking a prize, she thanked herself for ignoring critics who had called her music too weird, while Lux, issued last year, was lavishly praised.

Puerto Rican reggaeton pioneer Daddy Yankee received the person of the year honor, with Janet Jackson handing him a lifetime achievement award, and he performed favorites such as Gasolina and Con Calma, joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana. Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh became the first Indian artist to take the stage at the ceremony.

Milo J, 20, looked taken aback when he beat Karol G, Jorge Drexler, Carin León and Rosalía for record of the year; he finished the night with four trophies and paid tribute to Argentine folk music. ARIA VEGA was chosen best new artist, and Sara Schell songwriter of the year.
Lux is also regarded as a likely contender when the Grammy nominations are revealed next week, a sign of how far music in Spanish and other languages now reaches.

views.view: The BBC calls Rosalía's night historic and says her album Lux got rave reviews.

pro.en: Miss Universe Zimbabwe, Roseanna Hall, and several other African contestants could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure U.S. visas, with the 75th edition's winner due to be crowned on 24 November and Hall still without the documents needed to travel to the U.S. territory.

Zambia has already pulled its representative, Pamela Mubanga, a 25-year-old registered nurse crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October, with the national organization saying her situation stems from the presidential travel restriction rather than personal circumstances such as documentation, and adding that five other African countries face similar difficulties without naming them.

Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial U.S. travel restrictions introduced under Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026 and suspend the issuance of visitor, student, exchange and immigrant visas to their nationals while also imposing curbs on other categories of non-immigrant visas.

With contestants having begun arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration and fittings, pressure is mounting on Hall and on the representative from South Sudan, who wrote that it is "50/50 whether we will make it," while Hall said she is not alone in this predicament.

issues.title: Historic Ocean Liner SS United States Sunk to Make a Giant Reef
issues.gist: The SS United States, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, was sunk off Florida. It is now the world's largest artificial reef.
issues.gistKo: 한때 세계에서 가장 빨랐던 여객선 SS 유나이티드 스테이츠호가 플로리다 앞바다에 가라앉았어요. 이제 세계에서 가장 큰 인공 어초예요.

The county said the sinking started around 4 p.m., and the ship went fully under around 9 p.m. It now rests about 180 feet deep, about 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

pro.en: The SS United States, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, was scuttled off Florida on Wednesday to form the world's largest artificial reef. Okaloosa County officials said the sinking began around 4 p.m. and the vessel slipped fully beneath the surface around 9 p.m., settling at a depth of about 180 feet some 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

The descent began later than scheduled because crews first had to flood several very large tanks, and air trapped inside the hull slowed the process once more than a dozen valves were opened around 4 p.m. The county said it never uses explosives and relies on flooding instead, and a remotely operated vehicle and side-scan sonar confirmed that the ship came to rest upright, as intended.

Measuring 990 feet, the liner is longer than the Titanic and reached 44 mph in sea trials. Its maiden voyage in 1952 took just under three days and 11 hours across the Atlantic, a record that still stands, and it spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before the move south, while activists who campaigned to preserve it as a museum were unsuccessful.

Officials expect the reef to draw divers and anglers. The funnels and propeller were removed before the sinking, and a nonprofit conservancy intends to build a museum in Okaloosa County to display the ship's history, while a charter-trip observer said the site lies within a convenient range for fishing outings. Attention now turns to dives on the wreck and to how marine life colonizes it.

views.view: The BBC said the ship was sunk on purpose to make a reef, and activists failed to save it as a museum.
Local TV said county officials explained the delay and said the ship landed upright.
CNN described the sinking as a new chapter that gives the old liner a second life as a dive site.

lines.life: You could one day dive or take a boat trip to see how an old ship turns into a reef.

pro.en: A fleeting episode at Arlington National Cemetery drew wide attention this week, when a guard posted at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier rebuked a party that counted U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth among its members. It took place once a Veterans Day wreath-laying ceremony had ended.

The Pentagon subsequently announced that Hegseth had awarded the soldier, Specialist Thomas Iglesias, a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier."
Reporter Bernd Debusmann of the BBC walked through the reasons the party was rebuked, the history behind the tight rules on how visitors must behave, and the weight given to keeping the Tomb quiet.

For Korean readers, the episode illustrates the reverence many nations accord to sites honoring fallen service members, and attention now turns to how the public weighs the rules at such memorials. The incident also underscores that the rules at a memorial are meant to apply to every visitor, including the most powerful ones, and that silence is part of the respect shown there.

pro.en: A BBC correspondent toured one of Ukraine's biggest power stations, which a Russian ballistic missile struck head-on. The site is heavily damaged and crews are working against the clock to bring it back, though the broadcaster kept its name and location secret for security reasons.

Air raid warnings repeatedly interrupt the work. During the crew's four-hour stay, sirens sounded seven times, and staff had to stop and take cover every time. DTEK chief executive Maxim Timchenko said the plant can be properly repaired for just one to two hours a day, that Russian attacks this year are twice as large and strong, and that work on the plant will run at least until next summer.

Even as peace talks between Ukraine and Russia continue, intensified Russian attacks on the energy grid have left Ukrainians facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.

Officials warn that daily life for millions of Ukrainians could become impossible to sustain if electricity cannot be guaranteed for at least four hours a day, and some say in private that the country is already nearly there; certain households in Kyiv already live with outages lasting as long as 20 hours.

DTEK says its workers are in effect fighting to guarantee electricity this winter; in October the company restored power to more than 6.7 million households left in the dark by Russian shelling. The pace of repairs under continuing attack is the key variable to watch.

views.view: Ukrainians face planned power cuts, and officials fear life becomes unsustainable if power drops below four hours a day.
Workers can fully repair the plant for only one to two hours a day because of constant attack threats.

issues.title: Australian Cricket's Sandpaper Scandal Returns After a Star Player's Memoir
issues.gist: A new memoir has brought back the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in Australian cricket. Captain Pat Cummins held a long news conference to deny that he was involved.
issues.gistKo: 새 회고록 때문에 2018년 호주 크리켓의 공 훼손 사건이 다시 불거졌어요. 주장 팻 커민스는 긴 기자회견을 열어 자신은 관련이 없다고 말했어요.

paragraphs.en: A scandal in Australian cricket from eight years ago is back in the news. In 2018, during a Test match against South Africa in Cape Town, Australian players used sandpaper to change the condition of the ball. Three players admitted they were involved, and they received long bans. The case became known as "sandpapergate."
paragraphs.ko: 8년 전 호주 크리켓의 스캔들이 다시 뉴스에 나왔어요. 2018년 케이프타운에서 열린 남아프리카공화국과의 테스트 경기에서 호주 선수들이 샌드페이퍼로 공의 상태를 바꿨어요. 선수 세 명이 관련되었음을 인정했고 긴 출전 정지를 받았어요. 이 사건은 '샌드페이퍼 게이트'로 알려졌어요.

paragraphs.en: The new attention comes from a memoir by Usman Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January. In the book, which came out last week, he says the whole Australian team knew about the plan. He wrote that he wanted the team to take responsibility together. But he has refused to say who knew what, because he does not want a "witch hunt."
paragraphs.ko: 새 관심은 지난 1월 국제 경기에서 은퇴한 우스만 카와자의 회고록에서 시작됐어요. 지난주 나온 이 책에서 그는 호주 팀 전체가 그 계획을 알고 있었다고 말해요. 그는 팀이 함께 책임을 져야 한다고 생각했다고 썼어요. 하지만 그는 '마녀사냥'을 원하지 않는다며 누가 무엇을 알았는지는 말하기를 거부했어요.

sents.en: In the book, which came out last week, he says the whole Australian team knew about the plan.

paragraphs.en: Australian captain Pat Cummins answered questions for more than an hour in Sydney on Friday. He said he wanted to put the rumours about his involvement to rest. He called Khawaja's claims "vague" and said it was hard that a friend had put him in this position. Asked about a new investigation, he said that is a matter for Cricket Australia.

Steve Smith, who was captain in 2018, and Cameron Bancroft have not spoken publicly yet. Cricket Australia's chief executive, Todd Greenberg, has ruled out reopening its investigation. pro.en: A scandal that rocked Australian cricket eight years ago has resurfaced. In 2018, during the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town, Australian players used sandpaper to tamper with the ball; three players admitted involvement and were handed lengthy bans, and the affair became known as "sandpapergate."

The renewed scrutiny stems from a memoir by Usman Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January. In the book, released last week, he says the entire Australian team knew of the scheme and that he wanted the side to take collective responsibility, though he has declined to say who knew what, saying he did not want to start a "witch hunt."

Australia's captain, Pat Cummins, fielded questions for more than an hour in Sydney on Friday in an effort to put rumours of his involvement to rest. He dismissed Khawaja's claims as "vague," acknowledged his frustration that a friend had placed him in this position and said any fresh inquiry was a matter for Cricket Australia.

The fallout has split opinion. David Warner, who received the harshest punishment of the trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' news conference had "thrown him under the bus," while Steve Smith, the captain at the time, and Cameron Bancroft have yet to comment publicly. Cricket Australia's chief executive, Todd Greenberg, has ruled out reopening its investigation, and some fans say they are weary of the saga.

Professor David Rowe argues the episode still stings because Australia sees itself as "a nation of good sports," and he warns that telling the public "there's no more to see here" risks fueling conspiracy theories. It also lands at an awkward moment for a side that had a lacklustre series in South Africa last month and is beginning a busy summer.

pro.en: A week after most American states had tallied their midterm results, Alaska is still awaiting a call in its Senate race, a tight contest between the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, the former congresswoman Mary Peltola; officials expect to finish counting all eligible ballots on Nov. 18.

The delay stems partly from geography: Alaska is more than six times the size of the UK and is linked chiefly by water and air rather than road, so regional carriers such as Alaska Seaplanes ferry ballots from remote communities, alongside passengers, medicine and supplies, to Juneau, a capital accessible only by plane or boat.

Mail voting adds further lag, since ballots postmarked by Election Day may arrive up to 10 days later, or 15 days for overseas voters, and Charles Stewart, an election expert at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said officials had opted to err on the side of accuracy rather than rush.

Should no candidate clear 50% in the first round, authorities will invoke ranked-choice voting, redistributing ballots from the lowest-placed candidates to their voters' second preferences; the presence on the ballot of a second Dan Sullivan raises questions, though results released so far suggest a low probability that it alters the outcome.
President Donald Trump asserted this week that the Alaska Senate election had been rigged owing to the second Sullivan, and his administration is appealing a lawsuit that a lower court dismissed.

views.view: Alaska counts slowly because of long distances, mail ballots that arrive late, and a careful process, and the Senate race is still close.

pro.en: Fighting erupted in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which governed the northern region for decades, and Ethiopia's national army, reviving a civil war that officially ended in 2022. Federal forces entered the regional capital, Mekelle, within two weeks and met little resistance; hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.

Government officials and their supporters contend the war is effectively over and that what remains is to root TPLF elements out of the region. The TPLF rejects that account, characterizing its pullback from the towns as a strategic withdrawal, and its spokesman says the movement is preparing a major counteroffensive.

Residents told the BBC that fighting persists in central, northern and north-western Tigray, though the broadcaster cannot report from the region and verification is difficult. Analysts are split: Cameroon Hudson argues the TPLF has forfeited popular support and lacks the strength for a wider war, while commentator Yared Tibebu cautions that a protracted conflict is plausible given the movement's record of surviving reversals.

In September, seven rebel groups, among them the TPLF, announced the Alliance for Survival, aimed at toppling Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Yared sees the bloc as a source of added staying power, whereas Hudson doubts it will alter the balance of forces, and a Mekelle University scholar argues peace hinges on Addis Ababa addressing Tigray's sense of economic and political marginalization.

Ordinary Tigrayans say they are weary of politics and want only peace and a chance to rebuild. A Mekelle salon owner described trade as almost non-existent amid widespread hardship; whether the fighting spreads, and whether any negotiations emerge, are the developments to watch.
